value.overview: The Short-billed Dowitcher (Limnodromus griseus) is a medium-sized migratory shorebird in the sandpiper family. It breeds in northern North America and spends the nonbreeding season mainly along coastal areas of the United States, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America. It is named for its relatively short bill compared with the Long-billed Dowitcher, although bill length can overlap. The species is often seen feeding in groups on exposed mud.
value.classification: The Short-billed Dowitcher belongs to the family Scolopacidae, which includes sandpipers, phalaropes, and snipes. It is one of two closely related dowitcher species in the genus Limnodromus.
value.identification: This compact shorebird has a long, straight bill, medium-length legs, and a slightly rounded body. In nonbreeding plumage it is mostly gray above and pale below, with a white lower face and a distinct white stripe along the back and rump. Breeding adults are more strongly patterned, with rusty-orange underparts and dark barring on the back. Juveniles are brownish and crisply marked. It can be difficult to separate from Long-billed Dowitcher, especially in plain plumage.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds across tundra, boreal wetlands, and shallow ponds in Alaska and Canada, with some populations breeding in the northern United States. During migration and winter it uses coastal mudflats, estuaries, salt ponds, lagoons, flooded fields, sewage ponds, and other shallow wetlands. In Costa Rica it is a migrant and nonbreeding visitor rather than a resident or breeding bird. It occurs mainly at suitable coastal wetlands and mudflats on both Pacific and Caribbean slopes, including estuarine and salt-pond habitats.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, Short-billed Dowitchers are recorded as migratory visitors, especially during the boreal autumn and winter, with some passage during spring migration. They do not breed in the country.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in northern wetlands, including tundra ponds, marshes, and shallow lakes. The nest is a depression on the ground, usually concealed among low vegetation. The female generally lays a small clutch of eggs, and both adults may participate in incubation and care of the young. Chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves. Timing and nesting ecology vary among the species’ regional populations and subspecies.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on small aquatic invertebrates such as insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, mollusks, and worms. It may also take other small prey and occasional plant material. The bird typically forages in shallow water or soft mud by rapidly probing its bill up and down, often creating a distinctive repetitive feeding motion. It may feed alone but commonly gathers in loose flocks with other shorebirds.
value.behavior: Short-billed Dowitchers are active, social shorebirds that often rest and forage in groups. They frequently stand quietly during high tide and become more active as mudflats or shallow wetlands are exposed. When disturbed, flocks can make fast, twisting flights before settling again. Their calls are generally short and sharp. Like many migratory shorebirds, they depend on a network of breeding, stopover, and wintering sites across the Americas.

conservation.populationTrend: Declining. Available assessments indicate an estimated global decline of approximately 20–49% over the past three generations, although the causes and strength of decline vary among populations.
conservation.threats: Major concerns include loss and degradation of coastal wetlands, estuaries, mudflats, and other migration or wintering habitats; disturbance at feeding and roosting sites; pollution; climate-related changes to wetlands and food supplies; and potential mortality or displacement associated with renewable-energy infrastructure. Because the species migrates across many countries, threats can accumulate at multiple locations during its annual cycle.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore coastal wetlands, estuaries, salt ponds, lagoons, and inland stopover wetlands used by shorebirds. Reduce disturbance near feeding and high-tide roosting areas, keep dogs under control where required, and support responsible wetland management and climate adaptation. Birdwatchers can contribute sightings to well-curated monitoring programs such as eBird and participate in coordinated shorebird surveys, helping identify important sites and track population change.
